title: Augustine's Confessions
hook: a book about a life, written the whole way through as a prayer to God

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Cappadocians: Basil and the two Gregorys, finding words for one God in three persons. Your line was three and one. Did the words help, or did the mystery stay bigger than them? Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

A teenager and his friends climb into a neighbor's orchard at night and strip a pear tree. They aren't hungry. They have better pears at home. They take a bite or two and throw the rest to the pigs. Years later, the thief is a bishop named Augustine, and he can't stop asking why he did it. His answer is uncomfortable: because it was forbidden, and because his friends were there. He tells this story in a book called the Confessions. And here is the strange thing about the book. It isn't written to us. Page after page, it's written to God.

The Confessions open with praise, borrowing a psalm: great is the Lord, and greatly to be praised. Then comes the sentence that holds the whole book. In Pusey's old translation, Augustine says to God: "for Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." That's the map. Everything after it is Augustine telling how restless he was. He chased learning, success, and applause as a teacher of speech. He chased love, and loved badly. He tried one philosophy after another. Each one, he says, was a place he hoped to rest, and none of them held. The word confession here does two jobs. It means owning up: the pears, the pride, the people he hurt. And it means praise: confessing who God is. Augustine does both in the same breath, so the book reads like one long conversation, with him doing the talking and listening for an answer. The turn comes in a garden in Milan. He's weeping under a fig tree, sick of himself, when he hears a child's voice from a nearby house, chanting over and over: "Take up and read; Take up and read." He opens the letters of Paul where they fall, and reads: "put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make not provision for the flesh." He says the shadows of doubt fled away. Christians in different churches still read the Confessions, Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant. Some come for the conversion. Some come for the honesty. A bishop, writing down that he stole fruit to impress his friends.

Here's the practice: write one paragraph addressed to God. Settle, and breathe. Find a pen, or your phone. If you pray, begin the way Augustine does, speaking to God directly, and say one true thing about where you are today: what you're chasing, what you're tired of, what you're glad of. If you don't pray, write it as a letter you're not sure where to send. Don't polish it. Augustine didn't hide the pears. When the paragraph is done, sit with it and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Augustine's Confessions. The story of a restless life, told as a prayer: owning up to what he did, and praising the God he says he was looking for all along.
Your line: our heart is restless. Today, when you reach for your phone or the fridge without knowing why, pause once and ask what you're really looking for. Day one thousand two hundred forty-two.

howItsDone: Christians of different churches read Augustine's Confessions as a spiritual classic, and some keep a prayer journal in the same spirit, writing to God directly about their lives.

original.note: Latin: confessions. Augustine's title carries both senses, owning up and praising God.

trapdoor: what you thought: a confession is a list of sins.
what it means: Augustine owns up to what he did and praises God in the same breath, writing his whole story as a prayer.
what a scholar hears: in Latin Christian use, confessio meant both owning up to sin and praising God, and Augustine's title uses both.
